subject: Biology
title: The Action Potential
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Action Potential usable.

hook.text: Neurons communicate using tiny electrical spikes that travel along their axons at high speed.

buildup.text: At rest, a neuron is negatively charged inside. A stimulus flips the charge—that's the action potential.

discovery.text: Sodium ions rush in, the charge flips positive, then potassium ions rush out to reset it.

twist.text: Action potentials are all-or-nothing. A neuron either fires fully or not at all—no half signals.

climax.text: Myelin insulation lets some signals travel at 120 meters per second—faster than a race car.

punchline.text: All or nothing. That's how neurons fire.

quiz.question: What does 'all-or-nothing' mean for action potentials?
options: Neurons fire fully or not at all

details.summary: An action potential is the electrical impulse that travels along a neuron's axon when voltage-gated ion channels open in sequence. Sodium ions rush in to depolarize the membrane, then potassium ions flow out to repolarize it, propagating the signal at up to 120 meters per second.
details.whyItMatters: Action potentials are the fundamental unit of neural communication. Understanding them explains how nerve signals travel, how anesthetics block pain, and how diseases like multiple sclerosis disrupt neural function.
takeaways: Sodium influx depolarizes the membrane; potassium efflux repolarizes it
Action potentials follow an all-or-nothing principle with no partial signals
Myelin insulation speeds transmission through saltatory conduction

faq.question: What does all-or-nothing mean for action potentials?
faq.answer: A neuron either fires a full action potential or does not fire at all. There is no partial signal. Signal intensity is encoded by firing frequency rather than amplitude, a stronger stimulus causes more frequent firing, not bigger signals.

faq.question: How do local anesthetics block pain signals?
faq.answer: Local anesthetics like lidocaine block voltage-gated sodium channels in pain-sensing neurons. Without sodium influx, action potentials cannot initiate. The pain signal never forms, so it never reaches the brain, creating numbness in the affected area.
